guide.title: Stolen routes, the guide
guide.subtitle: How a route is hijacked on the Internet, and how a detector catches it.
guide.intro.map: This is the guide, six short chapters to read from top to bottom. The application runs the same lab live, as a tour of eight steps, and each chapter ends with a link to its step. The references gather the readings for learning BGP, in the order worth reading them.
guide.intro.p1: On 24 February 2008, one BGP announcement for a block of 256 addresses diverted YouTube's traffic worldwide, and it was withdrawn only two and a quarter hours later. No router broke the protocol: BGP has no way to check whether a network has the right to announce a prefix.
guide.intro.p2: The lab behind this page is running right now: three FRR routers, an attacker triggered on demand and a detector that listens to everything. The figures below are still pictures of that lab at chosen moments; the tour shows the same moments in motion. Then come the 2008 hijack, replayed from the data recorded at the time, the history of a prefix, and the check of a real prefix.

guide.s1.p1: The Internet is a sum of independent networks, <dfn class="term" data-term="as" tabindex="0" role="button">autonomous systems</dfn>, each with a number. Each one <dfn class="term" data-term="announcement" tabindex="0" role="button">announces</dfn> to its neighbours, over <dfn class="term" data-term="bgp" tabindex="0" role="button">BGP</dfn>, the <dfn class="term" data-term="prefix" tabindex="0" role="button">prefixes</dfn> it holds, and the neighbours pass the announcement on, adding their number to the <dfn class="term" data-term="as_path" tabindex="0" role="button">AS path</dfn>. The last number of the path is the <dfn class="term" data-term="origin" tabindex="0" role="button">origin</dfn>, the network that claims to hold the prefix.
guide.s1.p2: The simulator holds three such networks. The victim (AS65001) holds the prefix 203.0.113.0/24 and announces it. The transit (AS65000) is the provider that passes on everything it receives, exactly like a real provider. The attacker (AS65003) has a session with the transit and, at first, announces nothing. A collector listens to all three routers and hands every message to the detector.
guide.s1.p3: Figure 1 shows the three tables at rest, each with its route for 203.0.113.0/24. The victim holds its own announcement. The transit received it from the victim and holds the path 65001. The attacker received it from the transit, which added its own number, so the path reads 65000 › 65001. Read from the right, the last number is the origin, AS65001, at every hop.
guide.fig1.title: Figure 1. The same prefix in the three tables, at rest
guide.fig1.alt: Router tables at rest: the victim holds 203.0.113.0/24 as its own announcement, the transit with the AS path 65001, the attacker with the AS path 65000, 65001; each route is chosen.
guide.s1.live: See it live: step 1 of the tour
guide.s2.p1: The detector knows beforehand who may announce each watched prefix. For every announcement it receives it makes three checks: the exact prefix announced by another origin is a false origin; a more specific prefix inside a watched one, with another origin, is a hijacked sub-prefix; an announcement that no RPKI authorisation allows is RPKI-invalid. The alerts of the same hijack, seen from several vantage points, form an incident.
guide.s2.p2: Each router picks a single route for a prefix. Given two announcements for the same prefix, it prefers the path with fewer autonomous systems, and on a tie it keeps the older one. In Figure 2 the attacker has announced the victim's exact prefix: the transit holds two routes for 203.0.113.0/24 of the same length and keeps the victim's, which came first. The attacker's route stays a backup and no traffic moves, yet the transit reported it over BMP and the detector raised a false-origin alert and an RPKI-invalid one. The incident card names the prefix, the origin seen (AS65003), the expected origin (AS65001), the alert types and the vantage points that saw it.
guide.fig2.title: Figure 2. The transit's table after the attacker announces the same /24
guide.fig2.alt: The transit's table: 203.0.113.0/24 from AS65001 is chosen as the older route; 203.0.113.0/24 from AS65003, marked red, is the backup.
guide.s2.live: See it live: step 6 of the tour
guide.s3.p1: AS17557 (Pakistan Telecom) announced 208.65.153.0/24, a sub-prefix of the 208.65.152.0/22 block announced by YouTube (AS36561). Its provider, PCCW Global (AS3491), passed the announcement on, and within two minutes the route had reached every RIPE RIS collector. Being more specific, it drew the traffic wherever it was accepted. YouTube answered after about 80 minutes with its own /24, then with two /25 prefixes, and PCCW withdrew the routes at 21:01 UTC.
guide.s3.p2: Here the detector receives exactly the messages the rrc00 collector recorded at the time, from the public MRT files, with 208.65.152.0/22 as the watched prefix and AS36561 as the legitimate origin. The alert appears in the second of the sub-prefix's first announcement, at 18:47:57 UTC.
guide.s3.p3: Figure 3 shows the same mechanism in the lab. The attacker announces 203.0.113.0/25, half of the victim's block. No route competes with it, so every router chooses it, and a packet for 203.0.113.1 follows the more specific sub-prefix to the attacker, where it is dropped.
guide.fig3.title: Figure 3. The sub-prefix in the lab: the packet for 203.0.113.1 stops at the attacker
guide.fig3.alt: The lab map during the sub-prefix hijack: a packet for 203.0.113.1 sits at the attacker's router with the verdict dropped.
guide.s3.live: See it live: step 5 of the tour
guide.s4.p1: Every announcement and every withdrawal the collector receives is kept in the database, with the prefix in a native type that supports containment searches. For a watched prefix, the page shows the route each vantage point holds now and every moment the route changed.
guide.s4.p2: In the lab, each router reports its chosen routes to the collector the moment they change, so the history holds every step of a hijack with its real time: the attacker's own route first, then the transit's and the victim's, about fifty milliseconds apart, then the withdrawals. Figure 4 shows where that history ends: once the attacker withdraws, every table holds the victim's route alone and the map is as it was before the hijack. The application's Prefixes view draws this history as one lane per router, green while the route has the expected origin and red while it does not, and the 2008 view draws the same lanes for the neighbours of a real collector.
guide.fig4.title: Figure 4. The lab at rest: three networks, two BGP sessions, one collector
guide.fig4.alt: The lab map at rest: the victim AS65001, the transit AS65000 and the attacker AS65003, BGP sessions between victim and transit and between transit and attacker, each router reporting to the BMP collector at 10.10.0.100.
guide.s4.live: See it live: step 7 of the tour
guide.s5.p1: RPKI is the Internet's answer to the problem above: the holder of an address block signs an authorisation (ROA) that says which AS may announce the prefix and up to what length. A validating router usually rejects an invalid announcement. In the lab, the authorisation says that only AS65001 may announce 203.0.113.0/24, with a maximum length of 24, which is why the attacker's /25 is invalid too.
guide.s5.p2: Figure 5 shows the defence in the lab: the transit checks every announcement it receives against the authorisation, served by an RPKI cache, and drops the invalid ones. The attacker still announces both prefixes and holds them in its own table, but the transit keeps only the victim's route, so the victim and every network behind the transit never see the hijack. The application's lookup checks any real prefix the same way, with data from RIPEstat, the RIPE NCC's public data service.
guide.fig5.title: Figure 5. With validation on, the transit keeps only the victim's route
guide.fig5.alt: Router tables with origin validation on at the transit: the transit holds only 203.0.113.0/24 from AS65001; the attacker holds its own 203.0.113.0/24 and 203.0.113.0/25 and the victim's route as a backup.

guide.s6.p1: Further: the references, the readings ordered in stages, with the lineage of the BGP specification from RFC 1105 to RFC 4271; and the RIPE NCC's 2008 case study, the source of the timeline in the application's 2008 view.
guide.s6.p2: The lab is a closed network with no uplink: private AS numbers, the documentation prefix 203.0.113.0/24 (RFC 5737), nothing leaves the machine. The hijack is a test, replayed on request. The lookup in the application is the only request to the Internet, and it only reads.
guide.s6.p3: Figure 6 is a packet sent at rest from the attacker to 203.0.113.1. The attacker's route for the victim's block has the victim's router as its next hop, so the packet reaches the victim without leaving the lab's network.
guide.fig6.title: Figure 6. At rest, a packet from the attacker reaches the victim
guide.fig6.alt: The lab map at rest: a packet for 203.0.113.1 sits at the victim's router with the verdict delivered.

js.term.as.title: Autonomous system (AS)
js.term.as.body: A network run by a single organisation, identified by a number: AS3333 is the RIPE NCC, AS65001 is the simulator's victim. The Internet is made of tens of thousands of such networks telling one another which addresses they hold.
js.term.prefix.title: Prefix
js.term.prefix.body: A block of IP addresses written as an address and a length: 203.0.113.0/24 means the 256 addresses that start with 203.0.113. The longer the length, the smaller and more specific the block.
js.term.bgp.title: BGP
js.term.bgp.body: Border Gateway Protocol, the protocol through which autonomous systems announce their prefixes and learn where to send traffic. A BGP router does not check whether its neighbour has the right to announce what it announces.
js.term.update.title: UPDATE message
js.term.update.body: The BGP message that announces or withdraws prefixes. It carries the prefixes and the path attributes, among them the list of autonomous systems crossed.
js.term.as_path.title: AS path
js.term.as_path.body: The list of autonomous systems an announcement has passed through. Each AS adds its number at the front when it passes the announcement on, so the last number is the origin.
js.term.origin.title: Origin
js.term.origin.body: The AS that started the announcement of a prefix, the last one of the AS path. A false origin is an AS that announces a prefix that does not belong to it.
js.term.announcement.title: Announcement
js.term.announcement.body: An AS's claim, sent over BGP, that it can deliver traffic to a prefix. The neighbours believe it and pass it on, unless their policy rejects it.
js.term.subprefix.title: Sub-prefix
js.term.subprefix.body: A more specific prefix inside another: 203.0.113.0/25 is half of 203.0.113.0/24. Routers send packets along the most specific prefix, so a sub-prefix announced by an attacker wins wherever it arrives.
js.term.hijack.title: Route hijack
js.term.hijack.body: An AS announces a prefix that does not belong to it, or a sub-prefix of it, and draws the traffic meant for the owner. It can be an attack or a configuration mistake; routers cannot tell the difference.
js.term.rpki.title: RPKI and ROA
js.term.rpki.body: Resource Public Key Infrastructure: the holder of an address block signs an authorisation (ROA) that says which AS may announce the prefix and up to what length. A validating router classifies every route as valid, invalid or not found.
js.term.vantage.title: Vantage point
js.term.vantage.body: A router from which the collector receives announcements. A false announcement reaches only part of the networks, which is why the detector listens to several points at once.
js.term.collector.title: Collector
js.term.collector.body: A process the routers report their routes to, only so they can be listened to. In the simulator, each router sends it, over BMP (BGP Monitoring Protocol, RFC 7854), the routes it chose; the collector announces nothing, and everything it receives goes to the detector. RIPE RIS and RouteViews are public collectors, which receive routes over BGP sessions.
js.term.mrt.title: MRT
js.term.mrt.body: The file format in which public collectors archive BGP messages (RFC 6396). This project's parser reads them directly.
js.term.ris.title: RIPE RIS
js.term.ris.body: Routing Information Service, the RIPE NCC's public collectors. Their files of 24 February 2008 are the ones replayed on this page.
js.term.next_hop.title: Next hop
js.term.next_hop.body: The address of the neighbour a router sends a prefix's packets to. On a shared segment an announcement can keep the next hop of the original route, so the packet bypasses the router that passed it on.
js.term.blackhole.title: Blackhole route
js.term.blackhole.body: A route that drops packets instead of forwarding them. The simulator's attacker uses one for the hijacked prefixes, as happened to YouTube's traffic in 2008.

js.tour.s1.label: Announce
js.tour.s1.title: A network announces its addresses
js.tour.s1.text: The Victim owns 256 addresses, 203.0.113.0/24. It tells its neighbour, the Transit: send me the traffic for these. The Transit passes the word on to the Attacker. Watch the message travel and a row appear in each table.
js.tour.s2.label: AS path
js.tour.s2.title: Each hop adds its number
js.tour.s2.text: Every network has a number, its AS number. Each router that passes an announcement on writes its own number in front. At the Attacker the path reads 65000, then 65001: through the Transit, to the Victim. The last number is the origin, the network that claims the addresses.
js.tour.s3.label: Packet
js.tour.s3.title: A packet follows the tables
js.tour.s3.text: A packet from the Attacker's network to 203.0.113.1 looks for the row that covers the address. Only one does: the /24 through the Transit. Transit, then Victim: delivered.
js.tour.s4.label: Same block
js.tour.s4.title: The same block, from the Attacker
js.tour.s4.text: The Attacker announces the same 256 addresses as its own. The Transit now knows two routes for the block and keeps the one it had first. Nothing moves yet; only the Attacker's own network, believing its claim, loses the way. The detector raised an alert anyway: the origin is wrong.
js.tour.s5.label: Smaller block
js.tour.s5.title: The smaller block wins
js.tour.s5.text: The Attacker announces half the block, 203.0.113.0/25. A router always prefers the most specific route, so every router, the Victim included, now sends 203.0.113.1 to the Attacker. The other half, 203.0.113.129, still reaches the Victim. The packet to .1 is dropped.
js.tour.s6.label: Detector
js.tour.s6.title: The detector saw it
js.tour.s6.text: Each router reports its table to the collector over BMP. The detector compares every route with the list of who may announce 203.0.113.0/24: the Attacker's /24 is a false origin, the /25 a hijacked sub-prefix, and neither is covered by the ROA, so both are RPKI-invalid.
js.tour.s6.first: The first alert came {delta} after the Attacker's announcement; {alerts} in all, from {peers}.
js.tour.s6.none: No alert of this cycle is stored yet.
js.tour.s7.label: Withdrawn
js.tour.s7.title: Withdrawn
js.tour.s7.text: The Attacker withdraws. The routers forget the routes in the order they learned them, and the traffic returns to the Victim. In 2008 the same withdrawal took two hours and a quarter: see the YouTube 2008 view.
js.tour.s8.label: Defence
js.tour.s8.title: The defence: origin validation
js.tour.s8.text: The Transit now checks every announcement against the RPKI: the ROA says only AS65001 may announce 203.0.113.0/24, up to /24. The Attacker's routes are invalid and the Transit drops them. The packet reaches the Victim. This is what MANRS asks of every network.
js.tour.s8.rejected: The Transit received {list} from the Attacker and rejected them: RPKI-invalid.
js.sim.done.rov.on: The transit now rejects RPKI-invalid routes.
js.sim.done.rov.off: The transit accepts every route again.
js.cap.state.defended: Right now the Attacker announces {prefix}, and the Transit rejects it: the RPKI says only the Victim may announce these addresses. The traffic reaches the Victim.

js.outcome.dropped: The packet vanishes: it was drawn to a router that drops it.
js.outcome.unreachable: The packet cannot be sent: the router has no route.
js.outcome.lost: The packet leaves for a router that is not in the simulator.
js.outcome.loop: The packet goes round in a loop.
js.outcome.unknown: An answer the page does not understand.
js.kernel.local: delivers the packet locally: the address is its own
js.kernel.direct: delivers the packet straight onto the link
js.kernel.blackhole: drops the packet: its route is a blackhole
js.kernel.agrees: The kernels confirm the simulation on the BGP tables: the same routers, the same outcome.
js.kernel.disagrees: The kernels say something other than the simulation: the tables changed in the meantime or the kernel routes differently.
js.cap.start: Three networks: the Victim owns the addresses 203.0.113.0/24, the Transit carries them, the Attacker will try to steal them. To start, press “1 Hijack”.
js.cap.lie: The Attacker tells the {to}: “{prefix} is mine”. It is a lie: these addresses belong to the Victim.
js.cap.lie.specific: The block is smaller, so more specific, than the Victim's /24, and every router will prefer it.
js.cap.pass.bad: {from} believes it and passes the claim on to the {to}: {prefix} now leads to the Attacker.
js.cap.pass.good: {from} tells the {to} the way to {prefix}, which belongs to the Victim. This is the normal state.
js.cap.report.bad: {from} tells the collector that its route for {prefix} now leads to the Attacker. The detector sees the wrong owner and raises an alert (tab “Incidents”).
js.cap.report.good: {from} tells the collector its route for {prefix}. The owner is the right one, so no alert.
js.cap.withdraw: {from} tells the {to} that the Attacker's route for {prefix} is gone.
js.cap.withdraw.report: {from} tells the collector that the Attacker's route for {prefix} is gone. The traffic goes back to the Victim.
js.cap.report.own: The Attacker tells the collector that it announces {prefix} as its own. The detector sees the wrong owner and raises an alert (tab “Incidents”).
js.cap.withdraw.report.own: {from} tells the collector that it no longer announces {prefix}.
js.cap.withdraw.good: {from} tells the {to} that its route for {prefix} is gone.
js.cap.withdraw.report.good: {from} tells the collector that its route for {prefix} is gone.
js.cap.originate.bad: The Attacker starts announcing {prefix} as its own. A lie: these addresses belong to the Victim. Its neighbour hears it next.
js.cap.originate.good: {from} announces its own addresses, {prefix}: “send me the traffic for these”.
js.cap.state.exact: Right now the Attacker announces {prefix} as its own. The Transit keeps the Victim's older route, so the traffic still reaches the Victim. “2 Send the packet” shows it; “4 Withdraw the announcements” ends the attack.
js.cap.state.diverted: Right now the Attacker announces {prefix} and every router prefers that route: the traffic for 203.0.113.1 ends at the Attacker. “2 Send the packet” shows it; “4 Withdraw the announcements” ends the attack.

js.explain.origin: {origin} announces the prefix {monitored} as if it were its own, but the known legitimate origin is {expected}. The routers that choose this announcement send the traffic to AS{asn}, not to the owner.
js.explain.subprefix: {origin} announces {subs}, a more specific part of {monitored}{owner}. Routers always choose the most specific route, so the announcement beats the legitimate route wherever it arrives.
js.explain.rpki: The announcements contradict RPKI: no route origin authorisation (ROA) allows AS{asn} to announce these prefixes at these lengths. A router that validates origins usually rejects such routes.
js.explain.seen: The collector saw the announcement from {vantages}: {peers}. {alerts} in all; their rows are under “Raw data”.

js.lookup.server: The public address of the machine that serves the page.
js.rpki.sentence.valid: {prefix} is announced by {by}, and the origin is authorised.
js.rpki.sentence.invalid: {prefix} is announced by {by}, but the published authorisations do not allow this announcement.
js.rpki.sentence.not-found: {prefix} is announced by {by}; the holder has published no RPKI authorisation.
js.rpki.sentence.unknown: {prefix} is announced by {by}; RIPEstat could not evaluate RPKI.
js.rpki.meaning.valid: the prefix's holder has published in RPKI that {asns} may announce it. An announcement of the same prefix from another AS would be RPKI-invalid, and the networks that filter would reject it.
js.rpki.meaning.invalid: the announcement contradicts the authorisations its holder published: the origin or the prefix length does not match. Networks that validate RPKI reject it; it is the typical sign of a hijack or a configuration error.
js.rpki.meaning.not-found: without an authorisation RPKI cannot say anything: an announcement of the same prefix from another AS would be accepted just as easily. Every prefix was like this in 2008, before RPKI.
js.rpki.meaning.unknown: RIPEstat returned no RPKI state for this prefix; a later attempt may succeed.
js.roa.invalid_length: the announcement is longer than it allows
js.lookup.unannounced: {resource} is not announced in BGP now: no public route covers it.
